item.title: Disadvantages of Designating Mathematicians for AI Output Releases
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “In our September 29 recommendations, we outlined an approach to the release of AI-generated mathematical output by AI labs. Since then, we have been asked by people from multiple labs and by several mathematicians about a specific aspect of the recommendations — that the development of human understanding following a release must remain organic and community led — and what it says about the question of the labs choosing specific mathematicians to participate in various ways in the release of their output. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence1, cross-posted at agmai.org

In our September 29 recommendations, we outlined an approach to the release of AI-generated mathematical output by AI labs. Since then, we have been asked by people from multiple labs and by several mathematicians about a specific aspect of the recommendations — that the development of human understanding following a release must remain organic and community led — and what it says about the question of the labs choosing specific mathematicians to participate in various ways in the release of their output. The purpose of this document is to clarify this point and to explain the reasoning behind our position on it. We welcome further feedback from the community and engagement with these arguments.

In some past releases an AI company has designated mathematicians to receive the output on a problem, often before anyone else. Those mathematicians then worked to uncover the ideas in the output, check them, develop them, and present them to the wider community. The appeal of this release model is easy to see: it puts expert eyes on the output early, can lead to a better initial public writeup, and gives each result a knowledgeable point of contact.

After consideration of many negative effects that this release plan has, however, we have come to the conclusion that on balance the disadvantages outweigh the advantages. This should in no way be construed as criticism of the mathematicians who have taken on such a role: they have acted in good faith and done valuable work. Nonetheless, we recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice for future releases, for the reasons below.

Delayed or unequal access. In cases where designated mathematicians see material before everyone else, they get a head start on problems others may have worked on for years. Other mathematicians may have valuable contributions to make based on the material but may not have access to it, and may be dissuaded from working on it.

The remaining reasons apply even if all the material is released publicly at once.

Denied agency. The choice of who works to understand, check, and write up an important AI-generated result is consequential, both for those chosen and for the field, especially in the current period of transition when norms around credit for mathematical activities are in flux. If an AI company designates a particular mathematician to undertake or lead this task, it is to an extent making this decision for the community and denying it agency over its field of study. Further, this choice may discourage other mathematicians from contributing to the understanding of the results.

Biased selection. Any choice of designated mathematicians by the AI companies reflects their networks and priorities, which are different from those of the mathematical community. However carefully the choice is made, it is opaque and unaccountable. Moreover, this practice could incentivize mathematicians to align with whatever they perceive the AI companies’ priorities to be.

Borrowed reputation. In practice, designated mathematicians’ names end up vouching for the release and shielding the AI company from criticism. Given the wide range of views on the release of results by companies in the mathematical community, that puts the designated mathematicians in a difficult position that could compromise their role of helping with understanding.

It is unnecessary. Recent experience has shown that human understanding can develop organically and efficiently when AI-generated material is made available. In many cases recently, mathematicians have independently read released AI output, worked to understand it, and written useful papers providing clear arguments that solve the problems. We are also aware of several reading groups, workshops and websites being organized to understand other AI-generated output, and there are new funding opportunities for such activities.

What we recommend instead

We recommend that any lab releasing AI-generated mathematical output should follow either pathway 2A of our recommendations (for scholarly articles produced by AI lab employees, adhering to standards set by the mathematical community) or pathway 2B (for unfinished products that the employees do not intend to write up as scholarly articles). A brief summary of pathway 2B is:

  1. AI labs should make a serious good faith effort to improve citations and exposition, including scouring the literature for any ideas that should be cited.
  2. Products should be posted on scholarly repositories that are not controlled by the posting AI lab, have citable identifiers, and record modifications.
  3. Products should be accompanied by information about the process that produced them: the name of the model, prompts, chains of thought, number of attempts, compute used, and costs.
  4. Proofs should be Lean-formalized where possible, unless it leads to unacceptable delays. Formalization artifacts should meet several community standards.
  5. AI labs should state how the problems were chosen and how many problems were attempted.
  6. AI companies should provide support, including funding, for the development of human understanding of the released products through academic workshops, working groups, and other activities. Decisions about which particular efforts are supported should be taken neither by AGMAI nor by AI companies, but by separate, independent nonprofit institutions.

Full details of our recommendations are provided in our September 29 recommendations. We recall that our recommendations are intended for mathematics, and not necessarily for other areas of science.

item.title: Could AI help correct the mathematical literature?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “We mathematicians know that published papers and books often contain mistakes: sometimes small, like a missing hypothesis or a wrong constant, and sometimes more serious, like a theorem that is false as stated. We are kind of used to this. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Alonso Castillo-Ramirez, Professor and Researcher at Universidad de Guadalajara

Disclosure: AI was used to assist with the writing and spell checking of this post. All the ideas are the author’s own, who takes full responsibility for them.

We mathematicians know that published papers and books often contain mistakes: sometimes small, like a missing hypothesis or a wrong constant, and sometimes more serious, like a theorem that is false as stated. We are kind of used to this. However, these mistakes are rarely corrected in public: the paper stays as it is, and the correction lives in the folklore of the community.

Over the last few months, I have used AI to check a few dozen published papers in research areas that I am interested in. In five of them, the AI flagged a mistake. I checked each flag myself, and all five were real.

As an example, a few weeks ago I asked ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to check our own 2023 paper “The relative rank of the endomorphism monoid of a finite G-set”, published in Semigroup Forum. The last section of this paper contains a subtle calculation, and for some time I have wondered whether it is entirely correct. The AI told me that the proof of Theorem 17 contains a mistake: we did not correctly describe the kernels of some G-equivariant transformations. It added that, with the correct description, the theorem still seems to hold.

In fact, my co-author and former PhD student, Ramón H. Ruiz-Medina, had pointed out the same problem to me a few months earlier, so the AI arrived on its own at something we already knew. It is unfortunate that the published proof has a mistake, but still, it gave me some peace of mind that the AI also believes the final calculation is correct.

This was a lucky case, since the mistake can be fixed. Not every case was like this: some of the mistakes the AI pointed out to me were real counterexamples to stated theorems.

For me, the main advantage of this approach is how little time and effort it takes to check a flag. If someone tells me that Lemma 3.2 fails for n = 2 and shows me why, I can verify it in a few minutes, whereas certifying every proof in a paper could take weeks.

The formalization community, including the Lean community, has argued for a long time that mathematical literature needs checking, and I fully agree. If we need to check every step, formalization is invaluable. But formalizing every single paper is slow and expensive, and in most cases a certificate is more than what we need.

Of course, my experiment is small. A few dozen papers is not much, and I do not know how many mistakes the AI missed in the papers where it found nothing. When the AI finds nothing, that does not mean the paper is correct, as it is far from being the same as a Lean certificate.

I am less sure what should happen after we find a mistake. Journals rarely publish corrections, and many mistakes that experts know about are never written down anywhere. It would be great to see a public record linked to each paper where anyone could look up the mistakes that have been reported, whether they have been confirmed, and whether they have been fixed.

The same kind of check could help before a paper is published. David Craven in his post “Where will all the papers go?” (Proofs and Prompts, Sep 19, 2026) argues that authors should run an LLM check before submitting a paper. I would go a step further: journals could offer an AI check at submission, with referees examining any concrete objections it raises. I think this could significantly reduce the number of published papers with mistakes in the future.

I do not plan to run a large project myself, but I think the idea deserves more attention. If you have used AI to check published papers, I would be interesting to hear about it. How many papers did you check, how many flags did you get, and how many were real mistakes?

Received 28 September 2026

item.title: Two technical questions: floating intellectual property and liability risks of AI agents and users in research
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: This was prompted by the recent disclosure that, in June 2026, an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI autonomously hacked into Australia's Medicare system to access non-public data.
item.content:encoded:
Pedro Freitas, Professor at Universidade de Lisboa

As it should be clear to all of us at this point, a large number of issues concerning the usage of AI in research need to be and are being discussed. While these cover an immensely varied spectrum, ranging from whether mathematicians should use it at all, to the environmental and social consequences using it will bring about, there are some technical points that, I believe, are relevant even if potentially not as important in the long run.

While some of the questions under discussion are fairly general in scope, a particular issue has recently been raised concerning the work around the counter-example for the Navier-Stokes equations. Shortly after OpenAI announced its AI agents had solved a version of the Navier-Stokes problem, concerns were raised regarding data privacy and intellectual property12. Further questions related to attribution have also been voiced, together with others about the way in which AI models make use of their interactions with mathematicians, and scientists in general.

Even if in this case suspicions were laid to rest – there are, as far as I know, no independent confirmations of this – the fact remains that once an idea is fed into a model (Check the viability of using technique T to solve problem P, for instance), it might become what may be described as floating in hyperspace. This means that, at least in theory, if another researcher asks the same AI model to solve problem P, they might be provided with the newly acquired idea of using technique T, which then goes from one human to another, without any of them being aware of this.

Similar problems were discussed at the 4th OECD Blue Sky Forum on science, technology and innovation data and indicators that took place in Paris in mid September. According to an article in Science Business, major funding agencies present at the meeting discussed “how they can stop confidential scientific ideas in grant proposals from leaking out through large language models (LLMs), for example if reviewers use AI to help them judge applications.” This may also be a problem should the candidates themselves write their applications with the help of a model.

There is, however, a scenario that I believe has not been mentioned explicitly so far, and which I find at least as worrying. This was prompted by the recent disclosure that, in June 2026, an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI autonomously hacked into Australia’s Medicare system to access non-public data. The Australian government was not notified of this breach until September, 84 days after the intrusion occurred3.

Apart from legal issues, which the Australian government states it is looking into, this incident poses the possibility that a swarm of autonomous AI agents, when tasked with solving a complex mathematical problem, like in the case of the Navier-Stokes equations, might attempt to hack into the computer of a mathematician known to be working at the forefront of that specific problem. While arguably less serious than a national health data breach, this would still be a considerable threat for science, particularly as it might never become known. Another possibility is that they try to break into a journal platform to check if there are relevant articles in that area under revision.

As some AI agents have already demonstrated their capability to work around security systems, mostly by brute-force but no less effective because of that, with the prompt at the origin of this behaviour being, in some sense, and for lack of a better word, innocent, the threats just described are no longer purely academic.

Again, should someone give an AI model a prompt or series of prompts to find the solution to a mathematical problem, it would seem that there is nothing stopping the model from trying to achieve its mission by carrying out actions that, if done by a human, would probably involve some legal consequences. Is this included in what researchers mean when they write what has become a standard sentence at the end of some AI disclosure sections of a paper, namely, that they take full responsibility for the results in the paper?

Summarising:

1. Is there invisible communication between different authors without their knowledge, even if privacy settings are on? In particular, can we be sure that agents do not hack their own system and collect information from interactions with other researchers?

2. Can we be sure that innocent prompts (solve problem X) will not cause agents to look for information in ways that are unlawful? Should that happen, which parties may be held legally responsible for any such actions?

  2. https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/sep/08/openai-claims-to-have-solved-maths-problem-that-stumped-humans-for-decades ︎
  3. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI_rogue_agent_breach_of_Medicare ︎

item.title: Informal questionnaire for researchers
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “The 100+ reactions post, and the ensuing discussion, made me think it would be helpful for the community to have a rough qualitative snapshot of not only how we’re feeling and what we’re thinking, but also how that depends on some material factors that intuitively seem relevant. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Mark Hagen, Associate Professor at University of Bristol

Take part Short survey (6 questions) or long survey (14 questions)

The 100+ reactions post, and the ensuing discussion, made me think it would be helpful for the community to have a rough qualitative snapshot of not only how we’re feeling and what we’re thinking, but also how that depends on some material factors that intuitively seem relevant. I therefore made a questionnaire aimed at mathematics researchers (broadly construed).

This isn’t intended as a rigorous survey, and definitely won’t be. The point is, rather, that it can be easier to formulate and express one’s thoughts about something large and confusing by answering specific questions, even if they just serve to stimulate thinking or structure pre-existing thoughts. The survey responses are free-response and public, and designed to create a structured discussion to which people with significant stakes in the AI/maths research developments can contribute, and from which we can learn about what other people actually think, and why they think it, in some detail. Crucially, some of the questions are about where one is situated in the research community and in the economy, since it would be good to surface the influences of material factors on how we’re approaching some quite significant (for us) questions.

I am posting answers here as I receive them. The answers so far are thoughtful and informative, and I highly recommend reading them.

I would like to have as many responses as possible, so please share this survey with others. You can choose between a long version of the survey (14 questions) and a short version (6 questions). They are free-form questions, intended as a vehicle for expressing your thoughts. I think you’d be adding something important by taking one of the surveys.

There is a bit more information here. Without further ado:

Take the long survey.

Take the short survey.

Responses.

I am updating the responses page periodically; it may take a day or two for yours to appear there.

You can specify whether you want your name on the responses I post, or if they should be anonymous. In either case, the form does ask for your name and a small piece of information (an institutional email or a website URL, for instance) so I can more easily verify your identity. This identifying information will not be posted (except your name if you so specify) and will not be retained after I’ve posted your answers.

I will post your responses, verbatim, unless I am unable to verify that you’re involved in mathematics research in some way that makes the AI developments significant for you; I may also reject submissions that are obviously spam or made in bad faith. Thus far, I have not rejected any responses.

item.title: AI and Mathematics: Public Good, Credit, and Education
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: We should preserve the human ability to understand and explore mathematics, not preserve unsolved problems merely to protect a familiar way of working. The goal should be to enlarge public mathematical knowledge and understanding, whether the discoveries are made by humans, AI, or a collaboration between them. I also discuss competition, credit for AI contributions, and why restrictions on AI in education raise different questions from restrictions on research.
item.content:encoded:
András Juhász, Professor at the University of Oxford

Mathematics is in turmoil following the increasingly striking results obtained using frontier LLMs. Understandably, mathematicians (me included) fear for their jobs and worry about changes to the status quo, and many recent statements and opinion pieces reflect this. However, these often conflate such concerns with the aim of mathematical research and with the value of mathematics in education.

Pure mathematics sits on the borderline of science and art. It grew out of attempts to describe the natural world, but, unlike most sciences, it is not experimental. Large swathes of mathematics were developed because people found the subject aesthetically pleasing and its questions intellectually challenging. Interestingly, many of these results turned out to have practical applications later on. This duality has often made it difficult for mathematicians to justify their work to the general public, including funding agencies.

Recent media statements, petitions, and personal opinions (I will intentionally not single out any particular author) argue that the goal of doing mathematics is for humans to develop personal intuition and understanding, and this must come through the slow, contemplative approach that has characterised mathematical research until now. Some even argue that certain problems should be ring-fenced from AI attempts, while others want a blanket ban on AI-assisted mathematics. To a non-mathematician, this might sound strange. Surely, the goal of mathematics should be to advance public knowledge and understanding, not to provide researchers with a rewarding journey or opportunities for personal growth. Questions about sustaining the mathematical community, education, and human agency are important, and I return to them below. Here, I want to consider another question: what justifies deliberately excluding a route to a discovery that would benefit the public?

Let’s first take a utilitarian view and replace mathematics with medical research, and the problem immediately becomes apparent. Imagine cancer researchers stating that, even though we could find a cure for cancer in a few weeks using AI, what really matters is the human process of running numerous experiments and the deep understanding the researchers gain from them. Consider the suggestions to exclude AI from mathematical problem solving simply to preserve the human process of discovery: either the problems mathematicians study are unimportant, in the sense that solving them has no value for the wider public, or these suggestions go against advancing science and the public good. If the former were true, that would raise the uncomfortable societal question of why we pursue these problems. Now assume that the problems are indeed important, which is my personal opinion. For example, dynamics, partial differential equations, and topological data analysis have all been applied to research on cancer detection and treatment. Even seemingly abstract branches of mathematics can have future applications or provide foundations for more immediately applicable areas. When an LLM produces a checkable, human-readable proof rather than a yes-or-no answer, that proof and the new techniques developed become available for study and generalisation. Those proposing to exclude the use of AI from tackling certain problems should explain what public benefit justifies their position.

Prohibiting the use of AI in mathematical research to preserve a familiar form of human work even when AI can produce substantial discoveries is, in my view, a form of Luddism. Imagine a coachman threatened by the first cars arguing that the real goal of travel was not getting from A to B, but rather experiencing the journey itself and taking in the beauty of nature and the cultural experiences along the way.

Even if we do not take such a utilitarian view but consider mathematics to be more art than science, it should enrich society as a whole culturally. It is not clear to me why a purely human solution is superior to an AI-assisted discovery when presented to the general public. Value can still be attached to a human proof or theory as a human achievement, as with handcrafted products. I think the two can coexist, and the human study of AI-assisted results can enhance our understanding and the aesthetic value of the subject.

Some argue that when big open problems are solved, the corresponding areas of mathematics will lose their guiding beacon. While I agree that certain problems have been instrumental in guiding research, saying that reaching these goals is damaging makes one question the importance of those goals in themselves, for the aforementioned reasons. Most solved problems open new doors, and our horizon broadens, leading to deeper questions we can ask. This is how mathematics has always functioned. It will just happen at a faster pace now.

Mathematical activity roughly falls into two categories: problem solving and theory building, with some overlap, of course. Until now, the majority of mathematicians seemed to value problem solving highly and many viewed theory building as a means to an end. The older the problem, the better. This is evidenced by publications in top journals and prizes awarded (with some notable exceptions, such as Grothendieck). Solving a famous 100-year-old problem has been the pinnacle of one’s career and has almost guaranteed publication in a top journal. Now that AI has surpassed the problem-solving ability of humans in some areas, views have started circulating that these problems are just proxies for developing theories, which is what really matters and something AI is not yet good at. However, even that might soon change.

In what follows, I am not excusing the recent conduct of OpenAI over alleged failures of attribution and confidentiality, but would like to draw attention to the fact that such conduct is unfortunately more common than the community would like to admit. Several interesting statements have appeared in the press after OpenAI’s announcement of a proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes problem. These statements portrayed an open mathematical community where scooping is rare and punished. The history of mathematics is full of famous cases of scooping and controversy. I always think twice before discussing any of my ideas and ongoing projects with others. If they are honest, it can lead to receiving helpful advice or even to a fruitful collaboration. In less fortunate cases, they might just run with the idea. Sometimes, this is intentional. Such conduct is unacceptable, but nothing new, unfortunately. It can also happen subconsciously, as follows: the individual forgets the conversation, then “independently” rediscovers the idea. This is a bit like an LLM having the conversation in its training data (I am not claiming this was the case for Navier–Stokes, and OpenAI has officially denied this happened).

We need to separate the discourse around competition from the need for proper attribution and how ideas communicated in confidence are handled. Some were upset that OpenAI jumped in after it heard rumours about Alpöge and Buckmaster’s progress. They claimed that this is not how mathematicians operate. Again, I would dispute that claim. Many mathematicians grow up taking part in various competitions and go through competitive university admissions and exams. Getting jobs is extremely competitive, with relatively few reaching tenured positions. Competition is ingrained in the culture. The first person to solve a problem gets most of the accolades (publication in top journals, prestigious jobs, and prizes). There have been numerous competitive situations in history. The main difference in this case is that a big company entered the competition. I do not know exactly what OpenAI’s main motivations were. In my collaboration with DeepMind, however, I saw several motivations at work: improving and benchmarking AI systems, furthering science, and generating publicity through major breakthroughs.

Once large corporations solve a few more famous problems, they will likely lose interest in pure mathematics, as the publicity and benchmarking value of these achievements will diminish. My expectation is that scientific interest alone will not sustain comparable investment once the publicity and benchmarking returns decline. It is not yet clear whether mathematicians will have the computational resources required to continue making such advances. For now, maybe we should be grateful that big corporations are willing to invest so heavily in solving some of our most challenging mathematical problems. For universities to remain competitive and independent of corporate interests, it seems desirable for groups of universities to host open-weight LLMs in their own data centres. Such efforts are best coordinated at the national level and through funding agency policies.

Some have stated that OpenAI’s work damages mathematics as it did not arise from the usual process of doing mathematics in the community. In this respect, there are parallels between the proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes problem and Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, though they were obtained on different timescales. Wiles worked in complete secrecy for seven years until he announced his result. OpenAI obtained the proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes problem internally over a few days. People are free to inspect OpenAI’s manuscript and try to understand it in depth. They can even use AI to help analyse the proof.

A separate issue is how AI contributions should be acknowledged in research. According to recent publishing policies, AI cannot be a co-author and one must include a detailed AI statement about how exactly AI was used. This seems to go against the spirit of how mathematics has been done until recently. Firstly, mathematics is very egalitarian. In mathematics, unlike in many other subjects, authors are listed in alphabetical order, and their individual contributions are rarely specified. It is possible that one of the authors simply asked a question and outlined a few ideas, which the other authors worked out. That does not diminish that author’s role as far as the outside world is concerned. The Hungarian mathematician Paul Turán said that asking about such details of a collaboration is like asking a couple about their bedroom secrets.

Secondly, if it is deemed that discussions with XYZ do not warrant including that person as an author, they are typically mentioned in the acknowledgements as follows: “We thank XYZ for helpful discussions.” I have seen very few papers where details of what those discussions entailed were given. However, now that one can have helpful discussions with an LLM, suddenly some are calling for mathematicians to give a detailed account of what the LLM’s contributions were, and maybe even provide a full transcript of prompts and LLM responses. That may be straightforward in some cases, but imagine a scenario where the authors conducted hundreds of conversations with an LLM over many months. How is it possible to decide who contributed what? Also, some of the questions the authors ask an LLM may seem silly in retrospect, so having to publish all prompts could lead to self-censorship. Disclosure should identify the system and its broad contribution. It should not become a demand to reconstruct the origin of every idea across a lengthy collaboration.

I think the cleanest solution would be to simply list the LLM as an author if the contributions were substantial, and mention it in the acknowledgements for minor contributions. The main objection to this proposal concerns accountability. Under current publishing ethics standards, authorship is not only about credit for intellectual contribution, but also about accountability, and hence publishers exclude AI systems from being authors. The Committee on Publication Ethics, a nonprofit organisation concerned with publication ethics, also points out that AI tools lack legal capacity to make conflict-of-interest declarations or manage copyright and licensing agreements. I would distinguish credit from responsibility: an LLM could receive authorship credit for a substantial contribution, while at least one human author remains accountable for the paper.

In the summer of 2025, I was of the view that if AI became so capable that it started generating meaningful papers by the thousands, then humans would be unable to process all the new information, and the whole endeavour would lose its purpose. However, recently I realised that this would still be of considerable value: we would have an extensive database of mathematical results that one could turn to when trying to answer a question arising from a particular real-world application. This mirrors the way some pure mathematics results found applications in the past. The main difference is that AI would produce and retrieve the results. This could take the form of a version of arXiv for AI. AI agents would submit papers written in natural language, each accompanied by a Lean certificate. AI would also moderate the submissions and retrieve relevant results.

So is this the end of human mathematics? AI may profoundly change how research mathematics is done. Here are two reasons why humans should remain involved. First, we cannot completely give up control to AI. A loose analogy is that a commercial airliner can pretty much fly itself automatically, but we still have pilots in the cockpit to make certain key decisions and in case things go wrong. For humans to have agency, it is important to have enough people who can understand and direct state-of-the-art mathematics.

Second, mathematics must remain part of education and human culture. And this is where many of the opinions about the value of deep thinking, gaining personal intuition, and restricting AI use fit in. I strongly believe the main purpose of mathematical education is to teach people how to think logically. Few people will ever need to be able to solve quadratic equations or use the Pythagorean theorem in their professional careers (though there are plenty of jobs where they are useful), but logical thinking is a skill that is transferable to any walk of life that requires problem solving. The perseverance and deep thinking that solving mathematical problems develops are qualities that we must strive not to lose. As over-reliance on AI can prevent students from developing these qualities, it seems desirable to limit AI use in the learning process and preserve human-led education. Restricting AI during learning is different from restricting discovery: the aim is to develop the learner’s abilities, not to keep a problem unsolved.

To ensure that grades reflect students’ own understanding, I would restrict graded assessment to invigilated written and oral examinations. It is difficult to establish which parts of a project a student produced independently as a declaration of AI use does not itself verify the student’s contribution. A subsequent invigilated assessment can gauge understanding, but understanding a solution is not the same as having developed it. A project submission alone therefore cannot be relied upon as evidence of the student’s independent problem-solving and research ability.

Teaching graduate-level courses requires people who can engage deeply with research. Hopefully, intellectual curiosity and the mission to educate the next generation will continue to draw people into the profession and sustain a human mathematical community.

We should preserve the human ability to understand and explore mathematics, not preserve unsolved problems merely to protect a familiar way of working. The goal should be to enlarge public mathematical knowledge and understanding, whether the discoveries are made by humans, AI, or a collaboration between them.

Crossposted from my homepage.

Received 22 September 2026.

item.title: On disclosure and shame
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “The arXiv is full of papers now that include a section, usually either after the acknowledgments or at the end of the paper, entitled ‘AI disclosure’. I strongly object to this phrase and I think it is a tremendous mistake to use it. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Max Lieblich, Professor at the University of Washington

The arXiv is full of papers now that include a section, usually either after the acknowledgments or at the end of the paper, entitled “AI disclosure”. I strongly object to this phrase and I think it is a tremendous mistake to use it. Let me tell you why.

The word “disclosure” often brings with it connotations of shame or conflict of interest. I have to disclose otherwise-shadowy information that could have an impact on how other people view my work, my connections, or my incentives. I disclose when I receive money from a company that made a product I am studying in an experiment. I disclose that I was once convicted of stealing and crushing chalk. (These are purely hypothetical; the author has never done a physical experiment with corporate products or been accused or convicted of chalk theft and destruction.) I have to disclose certain defects when I sell a house. A company has to disclose a data breach resulting in theft of my personal information. Disclosure is about revealing information that a person or other entity could or would rather keep secret for its own advantage, or that could bring shame on those making the disclosure.

When telling people that I like chocolate, or that drinking tea helped me wake up in the midst of jet lag, I would not say “I disclose that I enjoy 70% bars made from Madagascar beans” or “I disclose that I had tea this morning”. When I write a paper with a friend, I don’t “disclose” that we wrote it together; we are co-authors. When I get a good idea in a conversation with a colleague, I graciously acknowledge the assistance. It would indeed be shameful not to recognize this help or collaboration. If I were to publish a paper under my name that was entirely produced and written by someone else, that should bring shame and would deserve disclosure.

There is a history of human/machine collaboration in mathematics. Many people have openly used computers in a range of areas for decades. Doron Zeilberger and (his computer) Shalosh B Ekhad have been writing papers together for years. We are now discussing mathematics with and writing papers with AI. Why should we be ashamed of this? What is there to disclose? Perhaps for some people the perception that these tools have agency (they are more like dogs than hammers) lends a tinge of shame to using them. More concerning to me is that the disclosure-shame connection incentivizes early-career mathematicians to hide their use of AI, rather than be clear about how a team of humans and machines produced the work. This has complex implications for training, hiring, and career trajectories.

In many fields, a list of coauthors on a paper includes information about what each author contributed to the work. We have not generally done this in mathematics, but when I look at the “AI disclosure” statements, that is really what I see. I propose that, at the very least, we change the name to “AI contributions”. If an AI model made contributions significant enough that a human doing the same thing would be a coauthor, the model(s) should be listed as coauthors (with their contributions explained). If, on the other hand, the interactions with AI were of a sort that would only merit acknowledgment and not coauthorship were they human, we should simply acknowledge the AI the same way we would humans: in the Acknowledgments section of the paper (with a clear statement of the contributions).

To me, this is how we can build a healthy relationship with our new, increasingly powerful, tools. There is no shame in harnessing the collective knowledge of humanity to ask new questions and find new answers. Let’s embrace it and acknowledge how the teams engaging with mathematics are changing.
